front: Why start with the simplest model?
back: It deploys earlier (validating the serving pipeline), is easier to debug, and is the baseline for complex models.
A benchmark winner may be too slow or costly, or no better on your data; prefer a simpler solution that works.

front: Majority vote of $n$ independent classifiers with accuracy $p$

back: Bagging: bootstrap samples, vote or average. Boosting: sequential re-weighting toward mistakes. Stacking: a meta-learner combines base learners.
Tracking records progress and results of runs; versioning records code, data, config and environment to reproduce them.
Sync waits for all workers (stragglers). Async updates as gradients arrive (stale gradients).
Data: copies of the model on different data shards. Model: different parts of one model on different machines (pipelining reduces idle time).
Random, simple heuristic, zero-rule (majority), human, and the existing solution.
$F_1=\frac{2pq}{p+q}$ and accuracy $=pq+(1-p)(1-q)$ for prevalence $p$ and positive-guess rate $q$.
Add realistic noise to test inputs and measure the performance drop; prefer models that stay accurate.
Change a field that must not matter (name, protected attribute) and count changed predictions.
Change an input in a way with a known effect direction (larger lot size cannot lower the price) and count violations.
Compute metrics on subsets of the data (mobile, region, rare class) because aggregates hide failures.
A model can win in every group yet lose overall because the groups have different weights in the totals.
Domain heuristics, error analysis, and automatic slice finders (beam search, clustering, decision trees).
